name: Tasmania
summary_text: Tasmania stands under the Australian national framework. The federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. A trans visitor to Tasmania can invoke that federal protection directly, and Tasmania is among the Australian jurisdictions whose vilification law also names gender identity as a protected ground. Federal hate-crime legislation in force since February 2025 expressly covers gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.  Male homosexual conduct ceased to be criminal in Tasmania with effect from 14 May 1997. The Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act commenced on 19 December 1994, but Tasmania kept its Criminal Code provisions until faced with a likely adverse outcome in Croome v Tasmania, at which point it repealed them and became the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. The age of consent is 17, a threshold shared only with South Australia.  Identity-document rules are permissive. In April 2019 Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill on 10 April 2019, after the Legislative Council had already approved it and after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove any requirement that a transgender person undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and allow people aged 16 or over to change their registered gender without parental approval. As of 2019 Tasmania also issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal.  Nothing in the sourced material imposes facility restrictions, medical screening or entry friction on trans travellers to Tasmania. Marriage equality has held nationally since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act came into force on 9 December 2017, federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and Tasmania allows same-sex couples to enter registered domestic partnerships with an optional official ceremony. Same-sex couples have had equal adoption rights in every Australian state and territory since April 2018.  No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern is documented for Tasmania, and the available evidence for trans equality there is enactment-level rather than case-level.

sources.documents: World-leading gender identity law removing surgery and divorce requirements, allowing self-declaration, non-binary/removal of gender, age 16 self-consent

name: Victoria
summary_text: Victoria stands under Australia's national framework on gender identity. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. No Victorian or Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017.  Victoria's own anti-vilification machinery was rebuilt by the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958 while repealing the Racial and Religious Tolerance Act, with the stated aims of equal participation and public safety. The Act carries gender identity as a ground but takes effect on 30 June 2026, and until that date Victoria's vilification coverage outside the federal layer extends only to sexual orientation. A visitor reporting gender-identity vilification in Victoria before 30 June 2026 therefore rests on the federal hate-crime offence rather than on state law.  Trans-specific mortality has been examined officially in the state. On 29 August 2024 ABC News reported that a Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people. The state government said it was reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups said they would press for their implementation.
